result: iBCI decoders degrade over time due to neural turnover, and recalibration imposes burdens on users. The authors establish the motivation for developing methods that stabilize decoders without recalibration by describing how iBCI decoder accuracy degrades due to neural turnover (C2), and how recalibration interrupts use (C17) and requires users to learn new decoder dynamics (C18).
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C16-C19 establish well-documented problems in the iBCI field based on general knowledge and citations. These claims provide the scientific rationale and motivation for the study but do not constitute novel findings.

result: Day-0 decoders trained on neural recordings show high within-day accuracy but consistently fail to predict motor outputs accurately on subsequent days across all tasks and monkeys. The authors collected data from six monkeys performing five tasks over 30-100 days (C67-C72), found substantial neural instability despite stable motor outputs (C73), and demonstrated that day-0 decoders had high accuracy on held-out day-0 trials (C76) but failed on day-k data (C77), with degradation occurring across all tasks and monkeys (C78).
evaluation: Claims C67-C78 describe the experimental setup and demonstrate decoder degradation with appropriate controls (within-day accuracy, motor output stability). The findings are supported by data shown in Figures 2 and supplementary figures with quantitative R² metrics.

result: The authors tested three alignment methods (Cycle-GAN, ADAN, and PAF) to address decoder degradation using GAN-based domain adaptation. Both ADAN and Cycle-GAN are static, causal methods that can be used in real-time (C82-C83), and hyperparameters were determined using the longest dataset then applied to all other datasets (C84-C85).
evaluation: Claims C79-C86 describe the experimental approach and methods tested. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate details about the properties of each method and the hyperparameter selection strategy.

result: Cycle-GAN works with full-dimensional neural recordings while ADAN and PAF require low-dimensional representations, and full-dimensional decoders perform better for Cycle-GAN while low-dimensional decoders perform better for ADAN and PAF. The authors found that full-dimensional decoders for ADAN and PAF were inferior to low-dimensional decoders (C90), while Cycle-GAN performed slightly worse with dimensionality reduction (C91), leading them to compare optimal configurations for each method (C92).
evaluation: Claims C87-C94 are supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing comparative decoder performance. The experimental design appropriately tests different decoder input formats for each alignment method, though the within-day accuracy differences are modest (R²=0.71-0.73, p=0.008).

result: Cycle-GAN significantly outperformed both ADAN and PAF in maintaining decoder accuracy, with the least performance degradation over time. On day-1, Cycle-GAN showed the smallest performance drop (-0.02±0.004) compared to ADAN (-0.06±0.005) and PAF (-0.11±0.005), all significantly different (p~0) (C95-C97). Over longer periods, Cycle-GAN had significantly less degradation than PAF (p=0.008) and better but not significantly so than ADAN (p=0.328) (C100-C101).
evaluation: Claims C95-C104 are supported by statistical analysis using linear mixed-effect models with appropriate sample sizes (n=2361) and controls. The results are shown in Figure 3 with quantitative metrics. The statistical tests are appropriate for the experimental design with multiple tasks as random factors.

result: When tested on continuous neural recordings without trial segmentation, Cycle-GAN showed clearly superior performance compared to both ADAN and PAF. On continuous recordings from monkey J, Cycle-GAN had significantly better day-1 performance (-0.05±0.015) than ADAN (-0.14±0.023) and PAF (-0.18±0.019), both p~0 (C110-C111), though all three methods showed similar degradation rates over time (p=0.56 for interaction) (C113).
evaluation: Claims C105-C113 are supported by statistical analysis (n=531 samples) shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3. This is an important practical test since real iBCI use involves continuous control. However, this analysis was only performed on one dataset (monkey J, isometric wrist task), limiting generalizability.

result: Cycle-GAN is more robust to hyperparameter settings than ADAN, particularly regarding batch size. ADAN performance dropped significantly with larger batch sizes (64: -0.13±0.0096; 256: -0.17±0.013; p~0) while Cycle-GAN performed consistently across all tested batch sizes (C119-C120). This allowed Cycle-GAN to use larger batch sizes (256 vs 8 for ADAN) for faster training (C123-C124).
evaluation: Claims C114-C126 are supported by systematic hyperparameter sweeps shown in Figure 4A-B with statistical testing (n=76). The analysis was limited to one dataset due to computational expense (C117), which is a reasonable practical constraint but limits generalizability of the hyperparameter recommendations.

result: Cycle-GAN is more robust to learning rate variations than ADAN. ADAN achieved good performance only with LRG of 1e-5 and 1e-4 but failed at 1e-3 (C130), while Cycle-GAN maintained stable performance at 1e-3 and 1e-4, with significant but still acceptable performance at 1e-5 (C131). ADAN required LRD ≤ LRG (C132) while Cycle-GAN remained stable across all tested LRD/LRG ratios (C133).
evaluation: Claims C127-C133 are supported by data in Figure 4C-D with statistical analysis (n=76). The inference time claim (C127) is supported by the architectural simplicity (two hidden layers, C128). However, like the batch size analysis, this was only tested on one dataset.

result: All three alignment methods require little training data, with performance plateauing around 40 trials. With only 10 trials, Cycle-GAN (-0.19±0.0076) and ADAN (-0.21±0.011) significantly outperformed PAF (-0.26±0.011), p~0, with Cycle-GAN significantly better than ADAN (p=0.003) (C139). Notably, ADAN and Cycle-GAN trained with 20 trials significantly outperformed PAF trained with 120 trials (p~0) (C140).
evaluation: Claims C134-C140 are supported by systematic testing with varying trial numbers shown in Figure 5 with statistical analysis (n=76). This is an important practical finding for clinical applications. However, this analysis was again limited to one dataset (Monkey J), limiting generalizability.

result: Both ADAN and Cycle-GAN successfully synthesize appropriate single-neuron activity patterns after alignment. The authors examined PETHs for individual electrodes and found that aligners appropriately synthesized activity for dropped-out neurons (E35, C152-C153), suppressed new activity (E73, C154-C155), and left stable neurons unchanged (E60, C156).
evaluation: Claims C141-C156 are supported by qualitative analysis of PETHs shown in Figure 6A. The examples demonstrate that the alignment methods can handle different types of neural changes. However, the analysis is limited to three example electrodes and lacks quantitative metrics for how well the synthesis matches day-0 patterns.

result: Both Cycle-GAN and ADAN substantially reduce between-day neural distribution differences as measured by MMD, with Cycle-GAN achieving significantly lower MMD than ADAN. Before alignment, between-day MMDs (1.42±0.029) were significantly larger than within-day MMDs (0.059±0.0054), p~0 (C158). After alignment, both methods reduced between-day MMDs to near within-day levels (ADAN: 0.19±0.0065; Cycle-GAN: 0.091±0.0024), with Cycle-GAN significantly lower than ADAN (p~0, n=171) (C159-C160).
evaluation: Claims C157-C160 are supported by MMD analysis shown in Figure 6B with appropriate statistical testing. The use of MMD provides a distribution-level metric complementing the decoder performance metrics. The analysis uses appropriate within-day controls and multiple kernel widths.

result: Alignment with Cycle-GAN or ADAN makes neural manifolds substantially more similar to day-0, with Cycle-GAN achieving high overlap. The authors used PCA and principal angles to show that unaligned day-k trajectories did not match day-0 (C165), but after alignment closely resembled day-0 (C166), with Cycle-GAN-aligned population subspaces showing high overlap (C171).
evaluation: Claims C161-C171 are supported by manifold analysis shown in Figure 7 using established methods (PCA, principal angles). The comparison to upper bounds from random subspaces (C168) and within-day bounds (C169) provides appropriate context. However, the analysis is primarily qualitative for the trajectories and could benefit from more quantitative metrics.

result: The authors' prior work with ADAN showed promise but was tested on limited data and showed sensitivity to hyperparameters. ADAN was previously shown to outperform CCA and KLDM (C49) but was only tested on one monkey, one task, for 2 weeks (C50), and subsequent exploration revealed sensitivity to hyperparameter settings (C51).
evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C45-C51, C172-C173 accurately describe the authors' prior work and its limitations, supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the rationale for the current study's broader testing and comparison with Cycle-GAN.

result: Overall, Cycle-GAN had the best performance and was easier to train and more robust than ADAN, making it ideal for stabilizing iBCI systems. Both GAN methods outperformed PAF (C65), cycle-consistency improved alignment and reduced hyperparameter dependence (C66), and Cycle-GAN was less sensitive to hyperparameters (C182) and superior with continuous data (C183), despite slower training than ADAN but faster than PAF (C181).
evaluation: Claims C8-C11, C62, C65-C66, C180-C184 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence from decoder performance, hyperparameter robustness, data efficiency, and neural alignment quality analyses. The conclusions are appropriately qualified regarding tradeoffs between methods.

result: The authors establish the conceptual framework and prior methods for neural alignment. They describe neural turnover as changing coordinates (C4), propose input stabilizers as a solution (C20), review prior methods including CCA (C22-C30), PAF (C31-C35), and domain adaptation with GANs (C36-C44), and explain Cycle-GAN's unique features including cycle-consistency (C54-C57) and full-dimensional alignment (C58-C61).
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C20-C44, C52-C64 provide background and conceptual framework supported by appropriate citations and established knowledge. These claims accurately describe prior work and the rationale for the current approach but do not constitute novel findings.

result: Multiple mechanisms contribute to neural recording instabilities, including electrode micromotion, extracellular environment changes, and neuronal state shifts, resulting in signal turnover on timescales of hours to days.
evaluation: Claims C12-C15 describe established mechanisms of neural instability supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context but represent prior knowledge rather than novel findings.

result: The study was motivated by uncertainty about ADAN's robustness and limited testing of PAF, leading to a comprehensive comparison including Cycle-GAN. The authors note that GANs are sensitive to hyperparameters (C174), PAF was tested primarily online in two monkeys (C175), and Cycle-GAN potentially offers advantages through bijective transformations (C178) and full-dimensional alignment (C179).
evaluation: Claims C174-C179 accurately describe the motivation and rationale for the study design, supported by appropriate citations and logical reasoning. These establish why the comprehensive comparison was needed.
